item.title: Higher Rates, Resilient Stocks and the Cash Flow Side of the Discount Rate
item.description: In a September 2026 post, Aswath Damodaran revisits how higher interest rates affect stock prices. He writes in the context of long-term Treasury yields at levels not seen in twenty years. The 10-year moved from 4.18%4.18\%4.18% at the start of 2026 to 4.75%4.75\%4.75% by the end of August. However, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq both rose strongly over the same eight months. Two ideas from his post are summarized here to explain how both can hold at once.

item.title: Firm Foundations and Castles in the Air
item.description:
In the opening chapter of A Random Walk Down Wall Street, Malkiel classifies nearly every approach to stock valuation as falling under one of two competing theories: the firm-foundation theory and the castle-in-the-air theory. He treats the two as close to mutually exclusive, and argues that understanding the gap between them is a prerequisite for avoiding serious investing mistakes.

The Firm-Foundation Theory

The firm-foundation theory holds that every stock has an intrinsic value, anchored to the underlying business, which a careful analyst can estimate from present conditions and future prospects. When the market price drifts away from that anchor, the theory says, it eventually snaps back, so the investor’s job is simply to compare price against calculated value and act on the gap. In modern terms, this is often referred to as reversion to the mean, and the intrinsic value is calculated by discounting future cash flows into present value. In other words, a dollar promised next year is worth less than a dollar today.

item.title: The Goldsmiths' Alchemy: The Origin of Paper Money
item.description:
Where did paper money actually come from? In Princes of the Yen, Richard Werner answers this by tracing it to a simple receipt slip, a piece of paper a medieval goldsmith handed over for gold left in safekeeping. That receipt is principally an ancestor to the bank note, and closely tied to the origins of paper money in Europe.

From Storage Slip to Money

Goldsmiths had the strongest vaults in town, hence people deposited their gold with them and in exchange were given a receipt as proof of the deposit. Carrying gold around town to settle payments was risky and cumbersome. As a result over time instead of withdrawing gold to make a payment, they just handed over the receipt itself, trusting that whoever received it could redeem it for gold. The receipt began circulating from hand to hand as if it were gold.

item.title: National Banking System before the Federal Reserve
item.description:
Previously I discussed how the North mobilized resources during the American Civil War. Salmon P. Chase did one more thing which led to the establishment of the national banking system in 1863 during the war. The subsequent challenges brought on by the system paved the way for the Fed.

National Banking System

Chase returned, for reasons I am yet to explore, to the idea of selling bonds. The bonds sold were of a special class with a 2% interest rate and a provision that these bonds could be used as collateral to allow banks to issue their own bank notes.

item.title: Financing during the American Civil War
item.description: In American monetary history, the creation of the Federal Reserve stands out as a monumental moment. To truly appreciate the importance and necessity of central banking, it is worth exploring the system that preceded the Fed. The period, prior to the Fed, was referred to as the National Banking System (1863-1913). The system was bereft with elasticity among other challenges that ultimately led to the creation of the Fed through the Federal Reserve Act. Before discussing the pre-Fed system I provide the context in which it emerged, namely the American Civil War.
